e-7198.knowledge_point: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral Over a Union of Type I Regions
e-7198.problem:
Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curves $y= 2^x,$ $y=\sqrt{x}$  and lines $x=0$ and $y=2,$ as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of a function $f(x,y)$ over the region $D$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/b80527fdef6f890581b8f56431e1b72a8f7eae3b41827caa16486ed9f2fd45ea.png)
e-7198.worked_solution:
The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions $D_1$ and $D_2,$ as shown below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/939e46b3ed4266f3c18d3567f951276e420292781cfc414711c244f453bc4029.png)

  

As a result, we get

$$
D_1 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x  \leq 1, \quad \sqrt x \leq y \leq 2^x \big\}
$$

and 

$$
D_2 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 1 \leq x  \leq 4, \quad \sqrt x \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.
$$

 

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{{2}^{x}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

e-7199.knowledge_point: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral Over a Union of Type II Regions
e-7199.problem:
Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curve $y=2+\ln x,$  and the lines $y=1$, $x=1,$ and  $x=e,$  as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of the function $f(x,y)$ over the region $D$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/4b0dff15fa9fa93ed61183702bff6bb443daf14b0adbf56cf4b97e3bd830ceea.png)
e-7199.worked_solution:
First, notice that:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2+\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⟹\,x={e}^{y-2}\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions $D_1$ and $D_2,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/2228ad860fea1e2c30d20bce749f654da02a97c65fd5e70152a07761e26f3e78.png)

    

As a result, we get

$$
D_1 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: 1 \leq y  \leq 2, \quad 1 \leq x \leq e \bigg\}
$$

and 

$$
D_2 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: 2 \leq y  \leq 3, \quad e^{y-2} \leq x \leq e\bigg\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{e}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{{e}^{y-2}}^{e}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

e-7197.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Over a Partitioned Region
e-7197.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/1d180fd5de88ebc465df522879142e5a4c5446c758aaccde792092968078c254.png)

The region $D$ is enclosed by the curves $x=2y^3-2y$ and  $x=y^3-4y,$ and the $y$-axis, as shown in the picture. Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm{d}A.$
e-7197.worked_solution:
The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions $D_1$ and $D_2,$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/6812e8036df171e162bee49d2edcff6d4a742e7bb4f14247713bd2332c64ccc6.png)

 

As a result, we get

$$
D_1 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: -2 \leq y  \leq 0, \quad 0 \leq x \leq y^3\!-\!4y \bigg\}
$$

and 

$$
D_2 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq y  \leq 1, \quad 2y^3\!-\!2y \leq x \leq 0 \bigg\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{3}-4y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{y}^{3}-2y}^{0}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}[x]_{0}^{{y}^{3}-4y}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}[x]_{2{y}^{3}-2y}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}({y}^{3}-4y)\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}(2y-2{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}-2{y}^{2}]}_{-2}^{0}+{[{y}^{2}-\frac{{y}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the lines y=−2x3, y=4x3 and y=x3+3, as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of the function f(x,y) over the region D as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.

a
∫−30∫x/3+3−2x/3f(x,y)dydx+∫03∫4x/3x/3+3f(x,y)dydx
b
∫−30∫x/3+3−2x/3f(x,y)dydx+∫03∫x/3+34x/3f(x,y)dydx
c
∫−30∫−2x/3x/3+3f(x,y)dydx+∫03∫4x/3x/3+3f(x,y)dydx
d
∫−30∫−2x/3x/3+3f(x,y)dydx+∫03∫x/3+34x/3f(x,y)dydx
e
∫−30∫4x/3x/3+3f(x,y)dydx+∫03∫−2x/3x/3+3f(x,y)dydx
Submit

decision.explanation: The intersections have x-coordinates -3, 0, and 3. Split at x=0: for -3≤x≤0 the lower boundary is y=-2x/3, and for 0≤x≤3 it is y=4x/3. The upper boundary is y=x/3+3 throughout. Thus option c gives both integrals with the correct bounds.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/797cddb4ea3cb41959df88e56517e9ee71e76e3cd08a9a93d2957b9792d14abb.png)

Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the lines $y=-\frac{2x}{3},$ $y=\frac{4x}{3}$ and $y=\frac{x}{3}+3,$ as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of the function $f(x,y)$ over the region $D$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.
after.worked_solution:
The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/0e69b1cb480b87216273db4336adff57cbf9d9bc450aac4b0cdb58b1ae63f6f7.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-3\le x\le 0,\,-\frac{2x}{3}\le y\le \frac{x}{3}+3}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 3,\,\frac{4x}{3}\le y\le \frac{x}{3}+3}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{0}{\int }_{-2x/3}^{x/3+3}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{4x/3}^{x/3+3}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the lines y=−2x3, y=4x3 and y=x3+3, as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of the function f(x,y) over the region D as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.

a
∫−30∫x/3+3−2x/3f(x,y)dydx+∫03∫4x/3x/3+3f(x,y)dydx
b
∫−30∫x/3+3−2x/3f(x,y)dydx+∫03∫x/3+34x/3f(x,y)dydx
c
∫−30∫−2x/3x/3+3f(x,y)dydx+∫03∫4x/3x/3+3f(x,y)dydx
d
∫−30∫−2x/3x/3+3f(x,y)dydx+∫03∫x/3+34x/3f(x,y)dydx
e
∫−30∫4x/3x/3+3f(x,y)dydx+∫03∫−2x/3x/3+3f(x,y)dydx
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The region D can be partitioned into two type I regions D1 and D2, as shown below.

As a result, we get D1={(x,y):−3≤x≤0,−2x3≤y≤x3+3}

and

D2={(x,y):0≤x≤3,4x3≤y≤x3+3}.

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain ∬Df(x,y)dA=∬D1f(x,y)dA+∬D2f(x,y)dA=∫−30∫−2x/3x/3+3f(x,y)dydx+∫03∫4x/3x/3+3f(x,y)dydx.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option c: on -3≤x≤0, y runs from -2x/3 to x/3+3; on 0≤x≤3, y runs from 4x/3 to x/3+3. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option e, not option c.

content.knowledge_point: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral Over a Union of Type I Regions
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/797cddb4ea3cb41959df88e56517e9ee71e76e3cd08a9a93d2957b9792d14abb.png)

Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the lines $y=-\frac{2x}{3},$ $y=\frac{4x}{3}$ and $y=\frac{x}{3}+3,$ as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of the function $f(x,y)$ over the region $D$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.
content.worked_solution:
The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/0e69b1cb480b87216273db4336adff57cbf9d9bc450aac4b0cdb58b1ae63f6f7.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-3\le x\le 0,\,-\frac{2x}{3}\le y\le \frac{x}{3}+3}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 3,\,\frac{4x}{3}\le y\le \frac{x}{3}+3}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{0}{\int }_{-2x/3}^{x/3+3}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{4x/3}^{x/3+3}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the curve y=x22+2, and the lines y=x+2, x=−2 and x=2. Express ∬Df(x,y)dA as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.

a
∫−20∫x+2x2/2+2f(x,y)dydx+∫02∫x2/2+2x+2f(x,y)dydx
b
∫−20∫x2/2+2x+2f(x,y)dydx+∫02∫x2/2+2x+2f(x,y)dydx

d
∫−20∫x+2x2/2+2f(x,y)dydx+∫02∫x+2x2/2+2f(x,y)dydx

decision.explanation: The curves intersect where x²/2=x, giving x=0 and x=2. On [-2,0], the parabola lies above the line; on [0,2], the line lies above the parabola. Splitting at x=0 and integrating from the lower curve to the upper curve gives option a.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curve $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2,$ and the lines $y=x+2,$ $x=-2$ and $x=2.$ Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.
after.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/019f0f9f83ddf323d543d109677335cb3ae72a200baf834453a0eca16a9353ba.png)

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/d222e86f6af7c3ed2b35711114c9062d6f0c9b0f2551aa44cac33318c6e5813f.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 0,\,x+2\le y\le \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2\le y\le x+2}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{x+2}^{{x}^{2}/2+2}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx+{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{{x}^{2}/2+2}^{x+2}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the curve y=x22+2, and the lines y=x+2, x=−2 and x=2. Express ∬Df(x,y)dA as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.

a
∫−20∫x+2x2/2+2f(x,y)dydx+∫02∫x2/2+2x+2f(x,y)dydx
b
∫−20∫x2/2+2x+2f(x,y)dydx+∫02∫x2/2+2x+2f(x,y)dydx
c
∫−20∫x2/2+2x+2f(x,y)dydx+∫02∫x+2x2/2+2f(x,y)dydx
d
∫−20∫x+2x2/2+2f(x,y)dydx+∫02∫x+2x2/2+2f(x,y)dydx
e
∫−21∫x+2x2/2+2f(x,y)dydx+∫12∫x2/2+2x+2f(x,y)dydx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's sketch our region.

The region D can be partitioned into two type I regions D1 and D2, as shown below.

As a result, we get D1={(x,y):−2≤x≤0,x+2≤y≤x22+2}

and

D2={(x,y):0≤x≤2,x22+2≤y≤x+2}.

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain ∬Df(x,y)dA=∬D1f(x,y)dA+∬D2f(x,y)dA=∫−20∫x+2x2/2+2f(x,y)dydx+∫02∫x2/2+2x+2f(x,y)dydx.

content.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curve $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2,$ and the lines $y=x+2,$ $x=-2$ and $x=2.$ Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.
content.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/019f0f9f83ddf323d543d109677335cb3ae72a200baf834453a0eca16a9353ba.png)

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/d222e86f6af7c3ed2b35711114c9062d6f0c9b0f2551aa44cac33318c6e5813f.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 0,\,x+2\le y\le \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+2\le y\le x+2}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{x+2}^{{x}^{2}/2+2}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx+{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{{x}^{2}/2+2}^{x+2}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The triangle has vertices (-2,2), (0,0), and (4,2). Split at x=0: the lower boundary is y=-x on [-2,0] and y=x/2 on [0,4], while the upper boundary is y=2 throughout. These bounds give option d.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the lines $y=-x,$ $y=2$ and $y=\frac{x}{2}.$ Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.
after.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/990f2180e92ffa9ae0b77a7c8c4aae284cacf03f7a7a62b1ed0b56f24705d671.png)

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/db7fe0aa7b746eab86c011545ec37d59d8f225f02a9fc6f4388754e1c528db8c.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 0,\,-x\le y\le 2}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,\frac{1}{2}x\le y\le 2}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-x}^{2}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx+{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{x/2}^{2}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the lines y=−x, y=2 and y=x2. Express ∬Df(x,y)dA as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.

a
∫01∫−x2f(x,y)dydx+∫12∫x/22f(x,y)dydx
b
∫−20∫−x2f(x,y)dydx+∫04∫2x/2f(x,y)dydx
c
∫01∫2−xf(x,y)dydx+∫12∫x/22f(x,y)dydx
d
∫−20∫−x2f(x,y)dydx+∫04∫x/22f(x,y)dydx
e
∫−20∫2−xf(x,y)dydx+∫04∫x/22f(x,y)dydx
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's sketch our region.

The region D can be partitioned into two type I regions D1 and D2, as shown below.

As a result, we get D1={(x,y):−2≤x≤0,−x≤y≤2}

and

D2={(x,y):0≤x≤4,12x≤y≤2}.

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain ∬Df(x,y)dA=∬D1f(x,y)dA+∬D2f(x,y)dA=∫−20∫−x2f(x,y)dydx+∫04∫x/22f(x,y)dydx.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option d. For -2≤x≤0, -x≤y≤2; for 0≤x≤4, x/2≤y≤2. Option b, which was deliberately submitted, reverses the second integral's y-bounds.

content.knowledge_point: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral Over a Union of Type I Regions
content.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the lines $y=-x,$ $y=2$ and $y=\frac{x}{2}.$ Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.
content.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/990f2180e92ffa9ae0b77a7c8c4aae284cacf03f7a7a62b1ed0b56f24705d671.png)

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/db7fe0aa7b746eab86c011545ec37d59d8f225f02a9fc6f4388754e1c528db8c.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 0,\,-x\le y\le 2}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,\frac{1}{2}x\le y\le 2}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-x}^{2}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx+{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{x/2}^{2}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the curve y=−6x2+24x−17 and lines y=6x−5, x=3, and y=1. Express ∬Df(x,y)dA as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.

a
∫12∫1−6x2+24x−17f(x,y)dydx+∫23∫1−6x2+24x−17f(x,y)dydx
b
∫12∫16x−5f(x,y)dydx+∫23∫1−6x2+24x−17f(x,y)dydx
c
∫12∫16x−5f(x,y)dydx+∫23∫17f(x,y)dydx
d
∫12∫16x−5f(x,y)dydx+∫23∫16x−5f(x,y)dydx
e
∫12∫17f(x,y)dydx+∫23∫1−6x2+24x−17f(x,y)dydx
Submit

decision.explanation: The line and parabola intersect at x=1 and x=2. Above y=1, the region's upper boundary is y=6x-5 for 1≤x≤2 and y=-6x²+24x-17 for 2≤x≤3, where the parabola returns to y=1. Splitting at x=2 gives option b.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curve $y=-6{x}^{2}+24x-17$ and lines $y=6x-5,$ $x=3,$ and $y=1.$
Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.
after.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/fe0209b3ed99aae4a1a939dfc7a8e0e400976809cc220abb1fbdf2f766c76171.png)

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/c8ba7d6923e2e4ef9ee528c48a8f5664ec10e4f05a13dad941713600d93ddfe5.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,1\le y\le 6x-5}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 3,\,1\le y\le -6{x}^{2}+24x-17}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{6x-5}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx+{\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{-6{x}^{2}+24x-17}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the curve y=−6x2+24x−17 and lines y=6x−5, x=3, and y=1. Express ∬Df(x,y)dA as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.

a
∫12∫1−6x2+24x−17f(x,y)dydx+∫23∫1−6x2+24x−17f(x,y)dydx
b
∫12∫16x−5f(x,y)dydx+∫23∫1−6x2+24x−17f(x,y)dydx
c
∫12∫16x−5f(x,y)dydx+∫23∫17f(x,y)dydx
d
∫12∫16x−5f(x,y)dydx+∫23∫16x−5f(x,y)dydx
e
∫12∫17f(x,y)dydx+∫23∫1−6x2+24x−17f(x,y)dydx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's sketch our region.

The region D can be partitioned into two type I regions D1 and D2, as shown below.

As a result, we get

D1={(x,y):1≤x≤2,1≤y≤6x−5}

and

D2={(x,y):2≤x≤3,1≤y≤−6x2+24x−17}.

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain

∬Df(x,y)dA=∬D1f(x,y)dA+∬D2f(x,y)dA=∫12∫16x−5f(x,y)dydx+∫23∫1−6x2+24x−17f(x,y)dydx.

content.problem:
Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curve $y=-6{x}^{2}+24x-17$ and lines $y=6x-5,$ $x=3,$ and $y=1.$
Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.
content.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/fe0209b3ed99aae4a1a939dfc7a8e0e400976809cc220abb1fbdf2f766c76171.png)

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/c8ba7d6923e2e4ef9ee528c48a8f5664ec10e4f05a13dad941713600d93ddfe5.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,1\le y\le 6x-5}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 3,\,1\le y\le -6{x}^{2}+24x-17}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{6x-5}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx+{\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{-6{x}^{2}+24x-17}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the curves y=ex, y=ln⁡x, and the lines y=1−x and y=1+e−x. Express ∬Df(x,y)dA as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.

a
∫01∫1+xexf(x,y)dydx+∫1e∫ln⁡x1+e+xf(x,y)dydx
b
∫02∫1−xexf(x,y)dydx+∫2e∫ln⁡x1+e+xf(x,y)dydx
c
∫01∫1−xexf(x,y)dydx+∫1e∫ln⁡x1+e−xf(x,y)dydx
d
∫02∫1−xexf(x,y)dydx+∫2e∫ln⁡xe−xf(x,y)dydx
e
∫01∫ln⁡xexf(x,y)dydx+∫1e∫1−x1+e−xf(x,y)dydx
Submit

decision.explanation: The boundary intersections occur at (0,1), (1,0), (1,e), and (e,1). For 0≤x≤1, the vertical bounds are 1-x≤y≤e^x. For 1≤x≤e, they are ln(x)≤y≤1+e-x. Splitting at x=1 gives option c.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curves $y={e}^{x},$ $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$  and the lines $y=1-x$  and $y=1+e-x.$ 
Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.
after.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/4854afc35aff7cfb47ba09481f975b22e41f3309b08a2ba7c409a4bbd32c8601.png)

  

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/50c5b7a864099f512515ab2db4c1596382883e93f7d4b23b9d16b91e42e3021b.png)

   

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,1-x\le y\le {e}^{x}}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le e,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x\le y\le 1+e-x}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-x}^{{e}^{x}}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx+{\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}^{1+e-x}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the curves y=ex, y=ln⁡x, and the lines y=1−x and y=1+e−x. Express ∬Df(x,y)dA as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.

a
∫01∫1+xexf(x,y)dydx+∫1e∫ln⁡x1+e+xf(x,y)dydx
b
∫02∫1−xexf(x,y)dydx+∫2e∫ln⁡x1+e+xf(x,y)dydx
c
∫01∫1−xexf(x,y)dydx+∫1e∫ln⁡x1+e−xf(x,y)dydx
d
∫02∫1−xexf(x,y)dydx+∫2e∫ln⁡xe−xf(x,y)dydx
e
∫01∫ln⁡xexf(x,y)dydx+∫1e∫1−x1+e−xf(x,y)dydx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's sketch our region.

The region D can be partitioned into two type I regions D1 and D2, as shown below.

As a result, we get

D1={(x,y):0≤x≤1,1−x≤y≤ex}

and

D2={(x,y):1≤x≤e,ln⁡x≤y≤1+e−x}.

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain

∬Df(x,y)dA=∬D1f(x,y)dA+∬D2f(x,y)dA=∫01∫1−xexf(x,y)dydx+∫1e∫ln⁡x1+e−xf(x,y)dydx.

content.problem:
Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curves $y={e}^{x},$ $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$  and the lines $y=1-x$  and $y=1+e-x.$ 
Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.
content.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/4854afc35aff7cfb47ba09481f975b22e41f3309b08a2ba7c409a4bbd32c8601.png)

  

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/50c5b7a864099f512515ab2db4c1596382883e93f7d4b23b9d16b91e42e3021b.png)

   

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,1-x\le y\le {e}^{x}}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le e,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x\le y\le 1+e-x}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-x}^{{e}^{x}}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx+{\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}^{1+e-x}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/a4515d2789a9b5c7a08210c0ef2611e7b6e661850b1fa822016b880427088bae.png)

Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{2},$ and the lines $y=2-x$ and $y=x,$ as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of the function $f(x,y)$ over the region $D$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.
after.worked_solution:
First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,x=-\sqrt{y} \\ y=2-x & \,⟹\,x=2-y \\ y=x & \,⟹\,x=y\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/78aa61f11856dbf35287a0af016b56744fec354d6c4e64690a1a6fe466f164e8.png)

  

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,-\sqrt{y}\le x\le y}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 4,\,-\sqrt{y}\le x\le 2-y}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{y}}^{y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-\sqrt{y}}^{2-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the curve y=x2, and the lines y=2−x and y=x, as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of the function f(x,y) over the region D as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.

a
∫01∫−yyf(x,y)dxdy+∫14∫−y2−yf(x,y)dxdy
b
∫01∫y−yf(x,y)dxdy+∫14∫−y2−yf(x,y)dxdy
c
 ∫01∫−yyf(x,y)dxdy+∫14∫2−y−yf(x,y)dxdy
d
∫01∫y2yf(x,y)dxdy+∫14∫2−yy2f(x,y)dxdy
e
∫01∫y2yf(x,y)dxdy+∫14∫y22−yf(x,y)dxdy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's write our equations in terms of y, as follows: y=x2⟹x=−yy=2−x⟹x=2−yy=x⟹x=y

The region D can be partitioned into two type II regions D1 and D2, as shown below.

As a result, we get D1={(x,y):0≤y≤1,−y≤x≤y}

and

D2={(x,y):1≤y≤4,−y≤x≤2−y}.

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain ∬Df(x,y)dA=∬D1f(x,y)dA+∬D2f(x,y)dA=∫01∫−yyf(x,y)dxdy+∫14∫−y2−yf(x,y)dxdy.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/a4515d2789a9b5c7a08210c0ef2611e7b6e661850b1fa822016b880427088bae.png)

Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{2},$ and the lines $y=2-x$ and $y=x,$ as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of the function $f(x,y)$ over the region $D$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.
content.worked_solution:
First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,x=-\sqrt{y} \\ y=2-x & \,⟹\,x=2-y \\ y=x & \,⟹\,x=y\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/78aa61f11856dbf35287a0af016b56744fec354d6c4e64690a1a6fe466f164e8.png)

  

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,-\sqrt{y}\le x\le y}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 4,\,-\sqrt{y}\le x\le 2-y}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{y}}^{y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-\sqrt{y}}^{2-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the curve y=ex, and the lines y=1−x and x=1. Express ∬Df(x,y)dA as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.

a
∫01∫11−yf(x,y)dxdy+∫1e∫ln⁡y1f(x,y)dxdy
b
∫01∫1−y1f(x,y)dxdy+∫1e∫ey1f(x,y)dxdy
c
∫01∫1−y1f(x,y)dxdy+∫1e∫1eyf(x,y)dxdy
d
∫01∫1−y1f(x,y)dxdy+∫1e∫1ln⁡yf(x,y)dxdy
e
∫01∫1−y1f(x,y)dxdy+∫1e∫ln⁡y1f(x,y)dxdy
Submit

decision.explanation: The curve and sloping line meet at (0,1). Horizontal slices have 1-y≤x≤1 for 0≤y≤1, and ln(y)≤x≤1 for 1≤y≤e. Thus option e gives the required type II integrals.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curve $y={e}^{x},$ and the lines $y=1-x$ and $x=1.$ Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.
after.worked_solution:
First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y={e}^{x} & \,⟹\,x=\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ y=1-x & \,⟹\,x=1-y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/0c61de3680b68dcf16267483fe1a51f0ef0e4c8247104215ae319d6c01b7a571.png)

  

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/c2a3cd01f74a2adb96e13212916dbb1b4476040d701ccd755258bd22fdefa5de.png)

  

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,1-y\le x\le 1}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le e,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡y\le x\le 1}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-y}^{1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}^{1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the curve y=ex, and the lines y=1−x and x=1. Express ∬Df(x,y)dA as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.

a
∫01∫11−yf(x,y)dxdy+∫1e∫ln⁡y1f(x,y)dxdy
b
∫01∫1−y1f(x,y)dxdy+∫1e∫ey1f(x,y)dxdy
c
∫01∫1−y1f(x,y)dxdy+∫1e∫1eyf(x,y)dxdy
d
∫01∫1−y1f(x,y)dxdy+∫1e∫1ln⁡yf(x,y)dxdy
e
∫01∫1−y1f(x,y)dxdy+∫1e∫ln⁡y1f(x,y)dxdy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's write our equations in terms of y, as follows: y=ex⟹x=ln⁡yy=1−x⟹x=1−y

Now, let's sketch our region.

The region D can be partitioned into two type II regions D1 and D2, as shown below.

As a result, we get D1={(x,y):0≤y≤1,1−y≤x≤1} and D2={(x,y):1≤y≤e,ln⁡y≤x≤1}.

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain ∬Df(x,y)dA=∬D1f(x,y)dA+∬D2f(x,y)dA=∫01∫1−y1f(x,y)dxdy+∫1e∫ln⁡y1f(x,y)dxdy.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option e: for 0≤y≤1, 1-y≤x≤1; for 1≤y≤e, ln(y)≤x≤1. The deliberately submitted option a reverses the first integral's bounds.

content.knowledge_point: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral Over a Union of Type II Regions
content.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curve $y={e}^{x},$ and the lines $y=1-x$ and $x=1.$ Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.
content.worked_solution:
First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y={e}^{x} & \,⟹\,x=\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ y=1-x & \,⟹\,x=1-y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/0c61de3680b68dcf16267483fe1a51f0ef0e4c8247104215ae319d6c01b7a571.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/c2a3cd01f74a2adb96e13212916dbb1b4476040d701ccd755258bd22fdefa5de.png)

$$

$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le e,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡y\le x\le 1}.

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-y}^{1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}^{1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the curves y=2x, y=x and lines y=1 and y=6−x. Express ∬Df(x,y)dA as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.

a
 ∫12∫2y2f(x,y)dxdy+∫24∫ln⁡2yy−6f(x,y)dxdy
b
 ∫12∫1y2f(x,y)dxdy+∫24∫log2⁡yy−6f(x,y)dxdy
c
 ∫1log⁡2∫log2⁡yy2f(x,y)dxdy+∫log⁡24∫2yy−6f(x,y)dxdy
d
∫12∫log2⁡yy2f(x,y)dxdy+∫24∫log2⁡y6−yf(x,y)dxdy
e
 ∫1log⁡2∫2y2f(x,y)dxdy+∫log⁡24∫2yy−6f(x,y)dxdy
Submit

decision.explanation: Rewrite the curves as x=log₂(y) and x=y², and the sloping line as x=6-y. The right boundary switches where y²=6-y, at y=2. The exponential meets the sloping line at (2,4). Thus the bounds are log₂(y)≤x≤y² for 1≤y≤2 and log₂(y)≤x≤6-y for 2≤y≤4, giving option d.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curves $y={2}^{x},$ $y=\sqrt{x}$  and lines $y=1$ and $y=6-x.$
Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.
after.worked_solution:
First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y={2}^{x} & \,⟹\,x={log}_{2}⁡y \\ y=\sqrt{x} & \,⟹\,x={y}^{2} \\ y=6-x & \,⟹\,x=6-y\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/fe95bc4ca8c687c79fe1c475eb1d8001d71a41ba34e076ad7fdfa8391cb08839.png)

   

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/099c35cbab4dfdd4a94207ed950fbdca8b8e766a612fb5e665e7d443d75ec050.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 2,\,{log}_{2}⁡y\le x\le {y}^{2}}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,2\le y\le 4,\,{log}_{2}⁡y\le x\le 6-y}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{{log}_{2}⁡y}^{{y}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{{log}_{2}⁡y}^{6-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the curves y=2x, y=x and lines y=1 and y=6−x. Express ∬Df(x,y)dA as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.

a
 ∫12∫2y2f(x,y)dxdy+∫24∫ln⁡2yy−6f(x,y)dxdy
b
 ∫12∫1y2f(x,y)dxdy+∫24∫log2⁡yy−6f(x,y)dxdy
c

d
∫12∫log2⁡yy2f(x,y)dxdy+∫24∫log2⁡y6−yf(x,y)dxdy
e
 ∫1log⁡2∫2y2f(x,y)dxdy+∫log⁡24∫2yy−6f(x,y)dxdy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's write our equations in terms of y, as follows:

y=2x⟹x=log2⁡yy=x⟹x=y2y=6−x⟹x=6−y

Now, let's sketch our region.

The region D can be partitioned into two type II regions D1 and D2, as shown below.

As a result, we get

D1={(x,y):1≤y≤2,log2⁡y≤x≤y2}

and

D2={(x,y):2≤y≤4,log2⁡y≤x≤6−y}.

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain

∬Df(x,y)dA=∬D1f(x,y)dA+∬D2f(x,y)dA=∫12∫log2⁡yy2f(x,y)dxdy+∫24∫log2⁡y6−yf(x,y)dxdy.

content.problem:
Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the curves $y={2}^{x},$ $y=\sqrt{x}$  and lines $y=1$ and $y=6-x.$
Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.
content.worked_solution:
First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y={2}^{x} & \,⟹\,x={log}_{2}⁡y \\ y=\sqrt{x} & \,⟹\,x={y}^{2} \\ y=6-x & \,⟹\,x=6-y\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/fe95bc4ca8c687c79fe1c475eb1d8001d71a41ba34e076ad7fdfa8391cb08839.png)

   

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/099c35cbab4dfdd4a94207ed950fbdca8b8e766a612fb5e665e7d443d75ec050.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 2,\,{log}_{2}⁡y\le x\le {y}^{2}}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,2\le y\le 4,\,{log}_{2}⁡y\le x\le 6-y}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{{log}_{2}⁡y}^{{y}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{{log}_{2}⁡y}^{6-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the lines y=x+6, y=2x, and y=3x, as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of the function f(x,y) over the region D as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.

a

b
∫09∫y/3y−6f(x,y)dxdy+∫912∫y/3y−6f(x,y)dxdy
c

d
∫09∫y−6y/2f(x,y)dxdy+∫912∫y/3y/2f(x,y)dxdy
e

decision.explanation: The vertices are (0,0), (3,9), and (6,12). Horizontal slices have right boundary x=y/2 throughout. The left boundary is x=y/3 for 0≤y≤9, then x=y-6 for 9≤y≤12. These bounds give option c.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/3fb6039f0a1de69d41644d7153d205062e85cdfce7cdb6b6270d952f2dbab6c3.png)

Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the lines $y=x+6,$ $y=2x,$ and $y=3x,$ as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of the function $f(x,y)$ over the region $D$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.
after.worked_solution:
First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2} \\ y=x+6 & \,⟹\,x=y-6 \\ y=3x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/c453d46a1f0cd6e6ddfa926de471fe38663df2bd86b9cdf4e58ce8d42462774a.png)

  

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 9,\,\frac{y}{3}\le x\le \frac{y}{2}}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,9\le y\le 12,\,y-6\le x\le \frac{y}{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{9}{\int }_{y/3}^{y/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{9}^{12}{\int }_{y-6}^{y/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the lines y=x+6, y=2x, and y=3x, as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of the function f(x,y) over the region D as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.

a
∫09∫y/36−yf(x,y)dxdy+∫912∫y/2y/3f(x,y)dxdy
b
∫09∫y/3y−6f(x,y)dxdy+∫912∫y/3y−6f(x,y)dxdy
c
∫09∫y/3y/2f(x,y)dxdy+∫912∫y−6y/2f(x,y)dxdy
d
∫09∫y−6y/2f(x,y)dxdy+∫912∫y/3y/2f(x,y)dxdy
e
∫09∫y−6y/2f(x,y)dxdy+∫912∫y−6y/3f(x,y)dxdy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's write our equations in terms of y, as follows:

y=2x⟹x=y2y=x+6⟹x=y−6y=3x⟹x=y3

The region D can be partitioned into two type II regions D1 and D2, as shown below.

As a result, we get

D1={(x,y):0≤y≤9,y3≤x≤y2}

and

D2={(x,y):9≤y≤12,y−6≤x≤y2}.

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain

∬Df(x,y)dA=∬D1f(x,y)dA+∬D2f(x,y)dA=∫09∫y/3y/2f(x,y)dxdy+∫912∫y−6y/2f(x,y)dxdy.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option c: y/3≤x≤y/2 for 0≤y≤9, and y-6≤x≤y/2 for 9≤y≤12. The deliberately submitted option d uses the wrong left boundary on both intervals.

content.knowledge_point: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral Over a Union of Type II Regions
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/3fb6039f0a1de69d41644d7153d205062e85cdfce7cdb6b6270d952f2dbab6c3.png)

Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the lines $y=x+6,$ $y=2x,$ and $y=3x,$ as shown in the picture. Express the double integral of the function $f(x,y)$ over the region $D$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.
content.worked_solution:
First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2} \\ y=x+6 & \,⟹\,x=y-6 \\ y=3x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/c453d46a1f0cd6e6ddfa926de471fe38663df2bd86b9cdf4e58ce8d42462774a.png)

  

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 9,\,\frac{y}{3}\le x\le \frac{y}{2}}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,9\le y\le 12,\,y-6\le x\le \frac{y}{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{9}{\int }_{y/3}^{y/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{9}^{12}{\int }_{y-6}^{y/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the lines y=−x, y=6−4x and y=2x. Express ∬Df(x,y)dA as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.

a
∫−20∫3/2−y/4−yf(x,y)dxdy+∫02∫y/23/2−y/4f(x,y)dxdy
b
∫−20∫6−4y−yf(x,y)dxdy+∫02∫2y6−4yf(x,y)dxdy
c
∫−20∫−y6−4yf(x,y)dxdy+∫02∫2y6−4yf(x,y)dxdy
d
∫−20∫−y3/2−y/4f(x,y)dxdy+∫02∫y/23/2−y/4f(x,y)dxdy
e
∫−20∫−y3/2−y/4f(x,y)dxdy+∫02∫3/2−y/4y/2f(x,y)dxdy

decision.explanation: The vertices are (2,-2), (0,0), and (1,2). The right boundary is x=3/2-y/4 throughout. The left boundary is x=-y for -2≤y≤0 and x=y/2 for 0≤y≤2. Thus option d gives the required type II integrals.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the lines $y=-x,$ $y=6-4x$ and $y=2x.$ Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.
after.worked_solution:
First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=-x & \,⟹\,x=-y \\ y=6-4x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4} \\ y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/08237d1ca2e01d0cf620dfa06a4265d8053b7ee34d0b65036aad7d5734726e1c.png)

 

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/c756dc7924fc4c116601da907eb3b767b8a40647e063c146dad83b0ea660933b.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le y\le 0,\,-y\le x\le \frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4}}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4}}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-y}^{3/2-y/4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y/2}^{3/2-y/4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed by the lines y=−x, y=6−4x and y=2x. Express ∬Df(x,y)dA as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.

a
∫−20∫3/2−y/4−yf(x,y)dxdy+∫02∫y/23/2−y/4f(x,y)dxdy
b
∫−20∫6−4y−yf(x,y)dxdy+∫02∫2y6−4yf(x,y)dxdy
c
∫−20∫−y6−4yf(x,y)dxdy+∫02∫2y6−4yf(x,y)dxdy
d
∫−20∫−y3/2−y/4f(x,y)dxdy+∫02∫y/23/2−y/4f(x,y)dxdy
e
∫−20∫−y3/2−y/4f(x,y)dxdy+∫02∫3/2−y/4y/2f(x,y)dxdy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's write our equations in terms of y, as follows: y=−x⟹x=−yy=6−4x⟹x=32−y4y=2x⟹x=y2

Now, let's sketch our region.

The region D can be partitioned into two type II regions D1 and D2, as shown below.

As a result, we get D1={(x,y):−2≤y≤0,−y≤x≤32−y4} and D2={(x,y):0≤y≤2,y2≤x≤32−y4}.

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain ∬Df(x,y)dA=∬D1f(x,y)dA+∬D2f(x,y)dA=∫−20∫−y3/2−y/4f(x,y)dxdy+∫02∫y/23/2−y/4f(x,y)dxdy.

content.knowledge_point: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral Over a Union of Type II Regions
content.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed by the lines $y=-x,$ $y=6-4x$ and $y=2x.$ Express ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA$ as a sum of repeated integrals over type II regions.
content.worked_solution:
First, let's write our equations in terms of $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y=-x & \,⟹\,x=-y \\ y=6-4x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4} \\ y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/08237d1ca2e01d0cf620dfa06a4265d8053b7ee34d0b65036aad7d5734726e1c.png)

 

The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/c756dc7924fc4c116601da907eb3b767b8a40647e063c146dad83b0ea660933b.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le y\le 0,\,-y\le x\le \frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4}}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{4}}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}f(x,y)\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}f(x,y)\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-y}^{3/2-y/4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y/2}^{3/2-y/4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 4,\,3-x\le y\le x-1}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2y\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}2y\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}2y\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{x-1}^{3-x}2y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{3-x}^{x-1}2y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,{|}_{x-1}^{3-x}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\,{|}_{3-x}^{x-1}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[(3-x)^{2}-(x-1)^{2}]\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}[(x-1)^{2}-(3-x)^{2}]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(8-4x)\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}(4x-8)\text{d}x \\  & =(8x-2{x}^{2}){|}_{1}^{2}+(2{x}^{2}-8x){|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =8(2-1)-2({2}^{2}-{1}^{2})+2({4}^{2}-{2}^{2})-8(4-2) \\  & =8-6+24-16 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ is enclosed by the the curve $y=(x-1)^{2}$ and the lines $y=x+1$ and $y=3-x,$ as shown in the picture. Evaluate ${∬}_{D}2y\,dA.$
after.worked_solution:
The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type I regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/f26c3e1bbbc268308db8d419bc799ad5349673e97c8828471997a5d36cb94d7d.png)

As a result, we get

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,(x-1)^{2}\le y\le x+1}
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,(x-1)^{2}\le y\le 3-x}.
$$

 

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2y\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}2y\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}2y\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{(x-1)^{2}}^{x+1}2y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{(x-1)^{2}}^{3-x}2y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}{|}_{(x-1)^{2}}^{x+1}\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}{|}_{(x-1)^{2}}^{3-x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[(x+1)^{2}-(x-1)^{4}]\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}[(3-x)^{2}-(x-1)^{4}]\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{(x+1)^{3}}{3}-\frac{(x-1)^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1}+{[-\frac{(3-x)^{3}}{3}-\frac{(x-1)^{5}}{5}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =((\frac{8}{3}-0)-(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{5}))+((-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{5})-(-\frac{8}{3}-0)) \\  & =\frac{32}{15}+\frac{32}{15} \\  & =\frac{64}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

The region D can be partitioned into two type I regions D1 and D2, as shown below.

As a result, we get

D1={(x,y):0≤x≤1,(x−1)2≤y≤x+1}

and

D2={(x,y):1≤x≤2,(x−1)2≤y≤3−x}.

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain

∬D2ydA=∬D12ydA+∬D22ydA=∫01∫(x−1)2x+12ydydx+∫12∫(x−1)23−x2ydydx=∫01y2|(x−1)2x+1dx+∫12y2|(x−1)23−xdx=∫01[(x+1)2−(x−1)4]dx+∫12[(3−x)2−(x−1)4]dx=[(x+1)33−(x−1)55]01+[−(3−x)33−(x−1)55]12=((83−0)−(13+15))+((−13−15)−(−83−0))=3215+3215=6415.

decision.explanation: D is the rectangle [0,3]×[0,3] with [0,2]×[0,1] removed. The integral over the full rectangle is 81, and over the removed rectangle it is 4. Thus the result is 81-4=77.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/13275042f8b7b74e394b3cee1350c19cfa50ddf63899066682cbd0109f42d6bf.png)

Evaluate ${∬}_{D}4xy\,dA,$ where $D$ is the region shown in the picture above.
after.worked_solution:
The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions ${D}_{1}$ and ${D}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070962/assets/648121ff2a676f6a472a6e221dffe813eca55f914aed0ca9a285bb0d4cd81ab3.png)

   

As a result, we get 

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,1\le y\le 3},
$$

and 

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le 3}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,dA & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}4xy\,dA+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}4xy\,dA \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}4xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}4xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[2x{y}^{2}]}_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}{[2x{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2x(9-1)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}2x(9-0)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}16x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}18x\,\text{d}x \\  & =8{x}^{2}{|}_{0}^{2}+9{x}^{2}{|}_{2}^{3} \\  & =8(4-0)+9(9-4) \\  & =77.\end{aligned}
$$
